title: Public Speaking and Presentation Skills
summary: Learn to manage nerves, structure a clear talk, use stories and simple slides, deliver with confidence, handle questions and speak well online.

lessons.title: Managing nerves with preparation and breathing

body.p: Almost everyone feels nervous before speaking to a group, including experienced teachers, pastors, politicians and presenters. A fast heartbeat, dry mouth and shaky hands are normal signs that your body is getting ready for something that matters. The goal is not to remove nerves. The goal is to use them and to stop them from running the talk.

Most fear comes from not knowing what will happen. You reduce that by preparing in three ways: know your opening by heart, know the order of your main points, and know your closing line. You do not need to memorise every word. If you know the first sentence and the last sentence, you can always start well and finish well, even if the middle wobbles.

body.h: A breathing routine you can use anywhere

steps: Sit or stand with your feet flat on the floor and your shoulders relaxed.
Breathe in slowly through your nose for about four counts.
Breathe out gently through your mouth for about six counts, longer than the breath in.
Repeat five or six times, then drop your shoulders and unclench your hands.
Take one more slow breath just before you start speaking.

body.p: Slow breathing gives you something calm and physical to do while you wait. It will not make you feel nothing, but many people find it steadies their voice.

Kwame must present a group project to his class on Friday. On Wednesday night he writes his opening sentence and closing sentence on a card and practises them aloud three times. On Thursday he practises the whole talk twice. On Friday, while waiting his turn, he does the breathing routine for a minute, walks to the front, and says his opening sentence slowly. Once the first sentence is out, he settles into the rest.

body.tip: Thoughts like 'everyone will laugh at me' are predictions, not facts. Replace them with a useful one: 'I am prepared, and the audience wants me to do well.' Most listeners are quietly on your side.

list: Write your opening sentence for any topic you know well and say it aloud five times.
Do the breathing routine for one minute and notice whether your shoulders feel looser.
Stand up and speak for one minute on 'my favourite meal' with nobody watching. Small, low-risk practice builds confidence.

body.p: A good talk is built for particular listeners. Before you write anything, answer two questions: who is listening, and what do I want them to think, feel or do afterwards? A talk with no clear purpose wanders. A talk that ignores the audience loses them, however well you speak.

body.h: Questions to ask before you prepare

list: Who will be there: classmates, parents, lecturers, community leaders, employers? How many people?
What do they already know about this topic, and what words might they not understand?
Why are they listening: because they must, because they are curious, or because they need to decide something?
How long do I have, and what is the room or platform like?
What is the one thing I want them to remember if they forget everything else?

body.p: Imagine you are speaking about online safety. To a group of Year 7 pupils, you might use simple words, a short real-life style example about a stranger asking for a photo, and a clear rule they can remember: 'Stop, block, tell an adult.' To parents at a school meeting, you might explain which apps pupils use, what warning signs to watch for, and how to talk to their children without causing panic. The topic is the same. The language, examples and the action you ask for are different.

Complete this sentence before writing your talk: 'After my talk, my audience will ____.' Good examples are 'understand how a bill becomes law', 'agree to donate books to our school library' or 'know three steps to prepare for an interview'. Keep the sentence on your desk while you prepare. If a story, fact or joke does not help that sentence, cut it.

body.tip: Avoid jargon unless you explain it. If you must use a technical word, give its meaning in plain English the first time you say it.

list: Choose a topic you know, such as how to save money as a student. Write two purpose sentences: one for your classmates and one for your grandparents.
List three words from your subject that an outsider might not understand, and write a plain-English meaning for each.

lessons.title: Structuring a talk: opening, three points and close

body.p: Listeners cannot go back and re-read a talk. They hear it once, so the structure must be simple enough to follow by ear. A reliable shape is: an opening that gets attention and states your purpose, three main points, and a close that repeats the key message and tells the audience what to do or remember.

body.h: The opening (about 10 percent of the time)

body.p: Start with something that makes people want to listen, then say what the talk is about. Options include a short question, a surprising fact you have checked, a brief story, or a clear statement of the problem. Avoid beginning with an apology such as 'Sorry, I am not very good at this'. It lowers the audience's confidence in you before you have begun.

Three is easy to remember and easy to deliver. Give each point a short label, one explanation, and one example. Use signposts so listeners know where they are: 'My first point is...', 'Now to the second reason...', 'Finally...'. If you have more than three ideas, group them or choose the three most important and drop the rest.
Say the key message again in one sentence, then end with a clear action or a memorable final line. Do not finish with 'That is all' or 'So... yeah.' Say 'Thank you', pause, and stop.

Most people speak clearly at roughly 130 words per minute, though this varies. At that pace, a 5-minute talk is 5 × 130 = 650 words. Because you will also pause, aim for a little under that. A 10-minute talk would be about 1300 words. Aisha has 5 minutes to persuade her class to start a reading club. Her plan is below.

body.code:
Opening (30 sec): 'How many of you read a book for fun last month?'
Purpose: 'I want you to join a weekly reading club.'
Point 1 (1 min 15): Reading improves vocabulary - example from English essays
Point 2 (1 min 15): It is free and friendly - example of swapping books
Point 3 (1 min 15): It fits our timetable - Friday lunch, 20 minutes
Close (45 sec): 'Join us this Friday. Bring one book you love.'

body.tip: Write your plan as key words on a small card, not as a full script. A full script tempts you to read, and reading makes your voice flat.

list: Pick a topic and write a plan in the same shape: opening, three points, close.
Time yourself speaking from the plan and compare it with your target length.

lessons.title: Stories, examples and making ideas stick

body.p: Facts alone are easy to forget. People remember a clear picture, a person or a short story much longer. Strong speakers use stories and examples to make each point real, so the audience can see the idea rather than only hear it.

list: It is short, usually under a minute for a short talk.
It has a person, a problem and an outcome.
It is specific: a named place, time or detail, not 'someone once did something'.
It is true, or clearly marked as an imagined example ('Imagine a student called Tunde...').
It connects directly to your point, and you say what the point is when it ends.

body.p: Compare two ways of supporting the point 'Saving small amounts adds up'. Vague: 'Many people save money and it helps them.' Specific: 'Last year my cousin put aside 500 naira every school day. By the end of the term she had enough to buy her own calculator for exams.' The second version is a picture. Because it is a story about one person, the audience can imagine it, so the idea sticks. Only use real details you are sure of, and change names if the story is about a private person.

body.h: Other tools: comparison, repetition, and the rule of three

body.p: A comparison links something new to something familiar: 'Your phone battery is like your energy; if you never recharge, it runs out.' Repetition of a key phrase helps people remember it. Lists of three feel complete and are easy to say.

body.tip: Be careful with statistics. Use a number only if you can name where it comes from, and explain it in plain words. Never invent a figure to sound impressive.

list: Choose one point from a talk you might give. Write a 4-sentence story that shows it: who, what happened, what changed, and what it proves.
Say it aloud, then cut any sentence that does not move the story forward.

lessons.title: Slides that help rather than distract

body.p: Slides are visual support. You are the main event. When slides are crowded, the audience reads them instead of listening, and then they are not really following either. A simple test: if the audience could understand the talk from the slides alone, you may not need to give a talk at all.

body.h: Rules that work on any phone or projector

list: One main idea per slide.
Use a short heading and no more than a few words or bullet points. Avoid paragraphs.
Use large, plain fonts that can be read from the back of the room. Sans-serif styles are usually clear.
Use strong contrast: dark text on a light background, or the reverse. Avoid colours that clash.
Use one clear image, chart or diagram instead of a wall of words. Make sure you have the right to use it, and label charts clearly.
Keep animations and sound effects to a minimum; they pull attention away from you.

body.p: Zainab's first slide on climate and farming has a title and 120 words in six bullet points. She improves it in three steps. First she chooses the single idea: 'Rain patterns are changing for farmers.' Second, she makes that the slide title. Third, she adds one photo of a dry field and moves her longer explanation to her speaking notes. The slide now supports her voice instead of competing with it.

steps: Save your slides in two places, for example your phone and a USB drive or email.
Export a PDF copy in case the software on the other device behaves differently.
Arrive early and test the screen, the clicker or laptop, and the sound.
Prepare a plan B: if the projector fails, can you give the talk using only your notes?

body.tip: Do not read the slide out loud word for word, and do not turn your back to the audience. Glance at the slide, then face the people and speak to them.

list: Take any slide or page of notes you already have and rewrite it with 10 words or fewer plus one picture idea.
Look at your slide from a distance of two metres. Can you still read it?

lessons.title: Voice, pace, pauses, eye contact and body language

body.p: Delivery is how your message is heard and seen. Good content can be lost if the audience cannot hear you, if you rush, or if you look at the floor. These skills improve quickly with practice, and you can train most of them alone.

Speak a little louder than feels natural, aim your voice at the back of the room, and slow down. Nervous speakers often rush. A comfortable pace for most audiences is around 130 words per minute. At 100 words per minute, a script of 300 words would take 3 minutes; at 130 words per minute the same script takes about 2.3 minutes. If your script is long, cut words rather than speeding up. Vary your tone so you do not sound like you are reading a list.

A pause of one or two seconds after an important sentence lets it land. It also gives you time to breathe and think, and it makes you sound confident. Replace filler words such as 'um', 'like' and 'you know' with silence. Silence feels much longer to you than it does to the audience.

Look at individual people for a full thought or sentence, then move to someone else, covering the left, middle and right of the room. Do not stare at the wall, the floor or only your teacher. If direct eye contact makes you anxious, look at foreheads or at friendly faces.

list: Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart and your weight even.
Keep your hands relaxed. Use open gestures when they fit your words; avoid fiddling with a pen or your clothing.
Do not pace or sway constantly. Move with a purpose, such as stepping towards a new point.
A natural smile at the start, when it suits the topic, helps the audience relax too.

steps: Stand in front of a mirror or a wall and read a paragraph aloud at your normal speed.
Read it again, 20 percent slower, with a two-second pause after each important sentence.
Record the second version on your phone and listen once. What sounds clearer?

body.tip: Choose just one thing to improve per practice session. Trying to fix voice, pace, hands and eye contact all at once usually fixes none of them.

lessons.title: Handling questions, speaking online, and practising with feedback

body.p: The last skills are what happens after your talk, how to adapt when the audience is on a screen, and how to keep improving. Together they turn one good talk into a lasting skill.

steps: Listen to the whole question without interrupting. Pause before you answer.
If the question is long, unclear or the room could not hear it, repeat it in your own words: 'So you are asking whether...?'
Answer briefly and honestly. If you do not know, say so: 'I am not sure, but I will find out and tell you.' Then do it.
Do not argue. If someone disagrees, thank them, say what you agree with, and explain your view calmly.
Check back: 'Does that answer your question?'

body.p: Before the talk, list five questions the audience is likely to ask and prepare short answers. Preparing for questions is one of the best nerve reducers.

list: Test your microphone and connection before the call. Close apps you do not need so the connection is steadier, and have your phone charged.
Sit with light on your face, not behind you. Place the camera at eye level.
Look at the camera lens when making key points. Looking at the faces on screen makes it seem you look away.
Speak a little more slowly and clearly than in a room, because sound can lag or cut out.
Use more variety in your voice, as there is less body language to rely on. Ask a question or use a quick poll to keep people involved.
Have a backup plan if data fails, such as sending your slides in advance.

body.p: Practise aloud, standing up, at least three times. Time yourself. If your talk is 5 minutes, practising it 3 times uses about 15 minutes, which is a small cost for a big improvement. Then record yourself on your phone and watch once. Choose one strength to keep and one thing to improve. Ask a friend or family member for feedback with specific questions: 'Could you hear me at the back? Which point was clearest? Where did you get lost?' Thank them, and try one change in your next practice.

body.tip: Feedback is information, not an attack. If a comment hurts, wait a day, then ask yourself what is useful in it.

list: Write three difficult questions about a topic you know and speak your answers aloud, each in under 30 seconds.
Record a one-minute talk. Watch it once and write down one thing to keep and one to change.

quiz.q: The night before a class presentation, Efua feels her heart racing and fears she will forget everything. Which action is most helpful?
options: Rewrite the whole script from memory again and again late into the night until she can say it with no mistakes
Practise aloud once or twice, make the opening and closing lines firm, do slow breathing, then rest
Avoid practising altogether so that she does not become more anxious before the talk
Tell herself that she must feel completely calm before speaking, or else the talk will fail

quiz.q: Just before standing up to speak, which breathing approach fits the routine in the lesson?
options: Take quick, shallow breaths through the mouth to wake the body up and raise energy
Hold the breath for as long as you can to calm the heart before you start
Skip breathing exercises, because they do not make any difference to nerves
Breathe in slowly through the nose, out longer through the mouth, a few times

quiz.q: You give a talk on mobile phone safety first to Year 7 pupils and later to their parents. What is the best adjustment?
options: Change the language, examples and the action you ask for so they suit each group
Use exactly the same talk for both groups, because the topic is the same
Use technical words with both groups, so that they see that you are an expert
Make the parents' talk shorter and drop the examples, since adults know the topic

quiz.q: You are given 5 minutes to persuade a committee to fund new school library books. What should you decide first?
options: Which colourful slide template and fonts you will use for the talk
How many jokes you can fit into the five minutes you are given
The one thing you want the committee to do or remember afterwards
Which long statistics you can quote from memory during the talk

quiz.q: Which is the best way to begin a talk on road safety for classmates?
options: 'Sorry, I am not very good at speaking, and I did not have much time to prepare, but I will try.'
Reading the title of the talk and your name aloud three times to settle the room
A short, relevant question or real-life example, then a statement of what the talk will cover
Starting in the middle of your first point without any introduction, to save time

quiz.q: Maryam has 5 minutes and has prepared nine separate points. What should she do?
options: Choose the three most important points and group or drop the rest
Keep all nine points and speak very quickly to fit them in
Cut the examples out so that there is time left for all nine points
Give the first four points then end with the words 'and many more'

quiz.q: You speak at about 130 words per minute and your talk must last 5 minutes. About how many words should your script contain?
options: About 1300 words
About 325 words
About 130 words
About 650 words

quiz.q: You want to make the point 'small savings add up'. Which support is strongest?
options: A statement that many people in your area save money and that it helps them a lot in many ways
A short story about one named person who saved a set amount daily and what it bought
A long list naming all of the banks in the country and their branches
A confident phrase such as 'as everyone knows, saving is good for you'

quiz.q: Your first draft slide has 120 words in six bullet points. What is the best fix?
options: Make the font smaller so that all six bullet points and the full detail still fit on one slide
Cut it to one main idea with a short heading and an image, and keep the detail in your notes
Read every bullet aloud word for word so that the audience gets all of the detail
Add animations so that the bullet points appear one at a time as you talk

quiz.q: Feedback from a friend says you rush and the audience cannot catch your points. What should you try?
options: Speed up even more to finish before the audience loses interest in you
Speak more quietly so that people have to lean in and listen carefully to follow every word
Remove the pauses and fill the gaps with 'um' and 'like' to sound fluent
Slow down slightly and pause for a second or two after important sentences

quiz.q: While presenting you notice you are reading from your page and rarely look up. What should you do?
options: Use key-word notes and look up at the end of each phrase, spending a moment with different people
Stare at the back wall of the room for the whole talk so that you do not get nervous or lose focus
Read the slides aloud to the audience instead, so that you do not lose your place
Hold the page higher in front of you so that it covers your face and your nerves

quiz.q: A listener asks a question you cannot answer. What is the best response?
options: Make up an answer that sounds confident, so that the audience does not doubt you or ask more
Tell the person the question is silly, then move on to a different topic
Say honestly that you are not sure, offer to find out, and follow up afterwards
Ignore the question and move quickly to the next hand that is raised

quiz.q: A questioner asks a long, confusing question and the people at the back may not have heard it. What should you do?
options: Answer a different question that you prepared earlier, which fits your slides
Say 'we do not have time for this' immediately and take the next question
Answer it in great detail for several minutes so that nobody is confused
Repeat or sum it up in your own words, check you understood, then answer briefly

quiz.q: You are giving a talk on a video call. Which choice helps most with connection with the audience?
options: Watching your own face on the screen the whole time to check how you look
Looking at the camera lens for key points and testing audio and connection beforehand
Turning off your microphone checks to save time before the call starts
Speaking faster since people online are impatient and may leave the call

quiz.q: After rehearsing, you record yourself on your phone. How should you use the recording?
options: Watch or listen once and choose one strength to keep and one specific thing to improve
List every single fault you can find and try to fix all of them by tomorrow
Delete it without watching, because hearing your own voice feels too uncomfortable
Watch it ten times in a row to memorise every word and gesture you made
